steps.q: A country has private ownership of capital, firms chasing profit, and prices set by free markets rather than the state. Who mainly decides what gets produced in such an economy?
steps.right: Private owners and buyers, through markets
steps.wrong: A central planning board, through orders

steps.q: A developing country moves workers out of subsistence farming into factory jobs and then office-based services. Do farm labourers and factory owners end up earning the same share of national income as before?
steps.right: No, the shares of income change between groups
steps.wrong: Yes, income shares stay the same for everyone
steps.hint: Think about who owns the new factories and who supplies the labour compared with farming.

steps.q: National income doubles over ten years, but almost all the extra income goes to factory owners and skilled workers while farm labourers' wages barely move. Has inequality definitely fallen just because the economy grew?
steps.right: No, growth can still leave inequality unchanged or worse
steps.wrong: Yes, growth always makes everyone more equal
steps.hint: Growth tells you the size of the pie grew, but does it tell you how it was sliced?

steps.q: A country's richest firms grow fast. Optimists claim that as owners spend and invest their extra profit, jobs and wages will eventually rise for poorer workers too. Does this always happen in practice?
steps.right: Not always, gains can stay concentrated at the top
steps.hint: Is spreading wealth from rich to poor guaranteed, or just one possible outcome economists debate?

steps.q: One country focuses on building factories to export manufactured goods; another focuses on capital-intensive mining for export. Would you expect ordinary workers to gain the same amount of income in both cases?
steps.right: No, it depends on which strategy is used
steps.wrong: Yes, any growth strategy spreads gains identically
steps.hint: Manufacturing usually employs many low-skilled workers, mining employs relatively few. Does that matter for who gains?
